sections.body: Egg quality depends on flock health, environment, collection hygiene, shell damage, and storage. Separate cracked, heavily soiled, or nonconforming eggs according to the facility system. Do not wash eggs or apply substances without authorization; handling must follow product requirements. Collect eggs gently and avoid pressure or mixing lots. Record production, nonconforming counts, and sudden changes. Report production declines along with intake and flock condition instead of covering them with outdated labels.

sections.body: Manage livestock waste to prevent contamination of water, feed, products, or surrounding areas. Storage and composting require plans for materials, moisture, aeration, and process monitoring. A pile does not become mature compost just because it has been sitting for a long time. Keep dirty routes separate from production areas and use dedicated tools. Report runoff and changes in odor. Workers must not mix chemicals or enter waste pits to speed up a task.

sections.body: Waste areas and confined spaces may contain toxic gases or low oxygen even when they look normal. Odor is not a safety meter. Do not enter or attempt a rescue by going down without a trained team and special procedures. Machinery, fans, pumps, and heaters also present electrical and fire risks. Know evacuation routes and how to call for help. When danger is present, stop work, move to a safe place, and report promptly rather than trying to meet production targets.
